title: "Soil resilience"
description: "Reading how soils organise themselves, and what that says about resilience and the many functions soils perform."

Soils are not random mixtures. They organise themselves over time, using and releasing energy as water, heat and carbon move through them, and that organisation is what lets a soil absorb shocks and keep doing many jobs at once. We measure it with thermodynamics rather than by counting soil types: pedodiversity reflects how a soil dissipates energy relative to what it has available.

In the U.S. Southwest, this approach revealed agroecosystem patterns on Indigenous lands, from the Chuska Mountains to the Great Sage Plain and Hopi land, where generations of land use and soil organisation are written into the landscape.

![From soil states with depth (A), to thermodynamic pedodiversity in three dimensions (B), to pedocomplexity (C): cultural insight and a physics-informed model, working together.](../images/soil-resilience-figure.jpg){fig-alt="Three-part graphical abstract: a depth curve of soil states, a three-dimensional block showing a cone of soil organisation narrowing with depth, and a colour scale listing enthalpy, entropy, exergy and free energy, with the caption cultural insight and physics-informed model."}
